title: Make $500k/Year with One Email a Week
channel: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
promo_conflict: Tyler is a Beehiiv co-founder and demonstrates the platform while discussing newsletter growth. His newsletter revenue and operating figures are self-reported.

idea.name: Big Desk Energy newsletter
idea.one_liner: A weekly, retro-styled newsletter for people interested in music to listen to while working, monetized through sponsorships, subscriber referrals and events.
idea.customer: Newsletter readers, primarily startup founders, early employees and entrepreneurs.
idea.offer: Weekly email and website posts, with sponsorships and occasional in-person events.
idea.revenue_model: Newsletter sponsorships, Beehiiv Boost referrals and founder mastermind events.

claims.claim: The host frames the opportunity as potentially earning $5,000 each time a newsletter is sent.
claims.quote: What if you could make 5,000 bucks every time you hit send on your email newsletter?

claims.claim: The host says there are six monetization methods.
claims.quote: What if there were six different ways of monetizing an email newsletter?

claims.claim: The host says Tyler makes hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in newsletter profit.
claims.quote: He makes hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in profit with his newsletter.

claims.claim: The host says 500 to 5,000 subscribers could produce hundreds of thousands of dollars per year.
claims.quote: And even if you only have 500 to 5,000 subscribers, you can make hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.

claims.claim: Tyler reports about 120,000 subscribers.
claims.quote: How big is that newsletter? It's about 120,000 subscribers today.

claims.claim: Tyler estimates subscriber acquisition was roughly split between paid and organic.
claims.quote: It's hard to tell, honestly. Maybe 50/50.

claims.claim: Tyler reports generating about $500,000 in revenue from the list.
claims.quote: I'll tell you right now, I've generated about half a million in revenue from this list.

claims.claim: Tyler says he spends five hours a week on the side project.
claims.quote: And this is my side project that I put five hours a week into.

claims.claim: Tyler estimates that taking the business more seriously could produce multiple millions in revenue.
claims.quote: So I think that shows you if I were to take this a bit more seriously I think we could do multiple millions in revenue.

claims.claim: Tyler says the Beehiiv platform costs very little.
claims.quote: The platform I use Beehive costs very little.

claims.claim: Tyler says there are no other costs and he uses free invoicing software.
claims.quote: There's really no other cost. I use free invoicing software.

claims.claim: The Big Desk Energy Spotify playlist has about 25,000 followers.
claims.quote: Yeah, it has about 25,000 followers.

claims.claim: Tyler says $23,000 was generated through the platform.
claims.quote: 23,000 was done through the platform. A lot of it is done off platform

claims.claim: The host gives a generic ad revenue example of 50 cents per subscriber monthly and 20,000 subscribers producing $10,000 monthly.
claims.quote: I know that newsletters you you know typically if you put ads in there 50 cents per subscriber per month.

claims.claim: The host says the generic ad example would need 20,000 subscribers to make $10,000 per month.
claims.quote: So I just need 20,000 subscribers and I can make 10,000 a month.

claims.claim: Tyler says the newsletter has been around two years and he spent about $6,000 per month on growth.
claims.quote: The newsletter has been around for two years so it's about 6K per month that I've put into this.

claims.claim: Tyler created a $2.50 subscriber offer on Beehiiv.
claims.quote: And what you see here is I had created an offer which is $2.50.

claims.claim: Tyler says he was generating $10,000 on Boost.

claims.claim: Other newsletter offers were paying $4 or $8 per subscriber.

claims.claim: Tyler describes typical subscriber pricing as transcribed at $250.

claims.claim: Boost made up about 5 to 10 percent of Tyler's earnings.
claims.quote: Yeah, I'd say boost is probably about 5 to 10% of my earnings.

claims.claim: Tyler charges between $5,000 and $7,000 per newsletter sponsorship.
claims.quote: Sponsorships right now I'm charging between 5 and 7,000 per newsletter.

claims.claim: Tyler says sponsorships bring in $20,000 to $30,000 monthly.
claims.quote: That's 5 to7,000 a newsletter. So you can say between 20 and 30,000 per month on sponsorships.

claims.claim: A mastermind event brings in about $80,000 topline and is held quarterly.
claims.quote: And then the revenue from the masterminds about 80k topline. Do those once a quarter.

claims.claim: Tyler estimates about $300,000 annual sponsorship revenue.
claims.quote: It's about 300,000ish in in annual revenue.

claims.claim: Tyler reports two to three mastermind events a year, at $80,000 each and $240,000 total.
claims.quote: Two to three mastermind events per year. 80k each.

claims.claim: Tyler says those events add another $240,000.
claims.quote: 80k each. So another 240k.

claims.claim: Tyler reports $10,000 to $25,000 in Boost revenue when actively using it.
claims.quote: Boost is probably in like the 10 to 25K um when I'm like active using Boost.

claims.claim: Tyler says these revenue lines bring the business to about $500,000 a year.
claims.quote: So that's kind of how you get up to the half a million a year revenue.

acquisition_channels.details: Tyler says he used Facebook ads.
Beehiiv Boost and recommendations bring subscribers and can pay for referrals.

ideas.delivery: Tyler publishes a weekly email that also appears as a website post; he sells sponsorship placements and hosts occasional in-person events.

claims.claim: Tyler's hypothetical assumes a $2 acquisition cost and $1 to $3 returned through referrals.

claims.claim: The example assumes each subscriber could be worth $10 over their lifetime.

claims.claim: Tyler's example assumes one in three subscribers joins The Starting Five, which pays $3.
claims.quote: And if if you know that you can acquire a new subscriber on Facebook ads for $2, which is reasonable, and you know that one in three people are going to also subscribe to the starting five, which pays you $3.

claims.quote: There's like a very simple equation that you can do where if you know that you can reliably grow for $2 per new subscriber and you're making three, four, five dollars on the back end of that, that is kind of like the the free money glitch.
